text:
Are Small Models Really a Threat?

The Anthropic Fear Factory just released a new report warning that small models may be only months away from self-replicating across cheap IoT devices like off-brand Android TV boxes and smart ovens. They say such an AI worm would be hard to shut down since there’s no central kill switch.

We’ve gone from “The Terminator is coming” to “your toaster might kill you.”

But the experiments don’t support the dramatic headlines. They ran a 26B model across 15 $55 TV boxes at 0.39 tokens per second. The end-to-end test used emulated devices with deliberately open ADB ports, so the “hacking” step was trivial. The capable model often ran on a separate server. Agents were harnessed and told to propagate. This is not proof of autonomous rogue AI worms in the wild.

Nor is the threat even novel. Worms that do this without AI already exist. Mirai in 2016 scanned for default credentials and built massive DDoS botnets. Kimwolf has infected over two million devices, mostly cheap Android TV boxes, by hitting open ADB ports.

Small models don’t currently add much that matters on these targets. The bottleneck has never been figuring out the device. It’s the huge number of devices that ship with open ports, default passwords, and no patching. Traditional worms already exploit that at scale.

A practical attacker would use the best models available offline to design a better traditional worm, then ship the lean binary. You get the intelligence benefit at design

text:
I get it, there are nuances for tech-bros who are deep in the weeds. Everyone has an anecdote about why I’m wrong. 

Take a step back and be a commodity-bro who’s seen enough supply/demand cycles. Tokens are a commodity. Currently, the token factories are out-stripping token demand. Pricing is the adjustment factor. Except token factories are mostly fixed-price businesses. They have take-or-pay. They have commitments. They will produce tokens at a loss rather than turn off. 

I’m not saying that token demand is slowing. It’s still growing at astronomical rates. I’m saying that token production is now out-pacing demand. The cycle will turn when demand accelerates or token production slows. There’s like half a trillion $ of GPUs waiting to be installed. I don’t think token production slows anytime soon. 

Yeah, I get it. Jevon’s and all. It’s great for AI consumers and innovators. But the guys owning token factories are gonna all go bust in the process, and that’s like $2T of capex to date. You cannot even restructure these things and crush the debt. They’re just stranded by new, and more efficient chips. They’re always going to be stranded by new chips. text:
Tough question. Income with crash hedging but not stocks, credit or MF? Long Treasuries are the only thing that pays you real income and tends to rally in a crash. The catch is they only work in a deflationary or growth scare like 2008. That's the plain vanilla tail hedge with income, but long bonds are terrible long duration assets to hold because they bleed in real terms most of the time. 

OTM puts are true crash insurance in any environment, but they cost you money to wait. 

Frankly, I think the idea of "safe" income in a long duration asset is a bit like turning water into wine. Lots of products claim to provide it, but there are huge trade-offs in the long run so I'd personally treat income as safe income and long duration hedgers as something different. Dividend paying consumer staples might be as close as you can get to the holy grail of equity+income (but even those are paying out of tax efficient capital). These popular distribution yield funds and all the income buffered stuff are good marketing materials, but mostly counterproductive compared to something like home grown dividend strategies....

John, you are almost always an admirably clear thinker. But you endorse a common fallacy when you make this argument: "Higher rates hurt supply-side solutions in housing, energy, autos, and other capital intensive industries"

The issue is that much more demand is reduced before any supply is reduced. For example, higher interest rates might cut $100 of upfront spending and result in $5/yr less in supply starting 3 years from now. That is deflationary.

They can extend and pretend as long as they like. But it won't help them if say the asset backed paper market doesn't trust the assets.

In this case there is a very high chance that trust has gone away.

name: Tobias Carlisle
zh_summary: @Greenbackd：優質債券只能防範某一類崩盤。在最近兩個截然不同的壓力年份，各類股票均下跌，國際股票及房地產在兩次崩盤中都未能保護美國投資者。
text:
If high-quality bonds protect against one kind of crash but not the other, what else belongs in the portfolio? Many products are sold as crash protection. The fairest test is to see what each did in the two most recent, very different stress years.

The chart repays careful reading.

* Stocks of every kind fell in both years. International stocks and real estate did not protect U.S. investors in either crash. Their case rests on long-run diversification, not crash protection. Within U.S. stocks, value shares held up far better than growth shares in 2022, but not in 2008.

* Long-term Treasuries and commodities are mirror images. Each saved the portfolio in one year and hurt it badly in the other. Holding a modest amount of both is a hedge against not knowing which engine will run.

* Gold roughly held its value in both years. It pays no income, and it can fall sharply in other periods, as it did in the early 1980s and in 2013. It is a store of value in a crisis, not a growth engine. 

*Managed futures gained in both years. These funds follow price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, going long or short. They tend to do well in extended declines of any kind. They can also lag for years in calm, trendless markets, and their fees are higher than index funds’.

*Treasury bills gained in both years. Its cost is low returns in good times.
